DeceptiWAF Shield · v1.4
~ built with sleep deprivation & way too much caffine — 01 / 19
Good afternoon, everyone — I'm Aryan Karan from the Computer Science & Engineering department at Kalyani University, and this project was supervised by Prof. Sukanta Majumder. Thank you for being here. So — what is DeceptiWAF? In plain language: it's a Web Application Firewall that doesn't just block bad traffic. It actively tricks attackers by silently routing them into a fake student portal, so they keep pounding on a decoy while we capture every payload, every IP, every fingerprint. The system rests on three technical pillars — AST lexical parsing for semantic SQLi/XSS detection, sliding-window rate limiting that closes boundary-burst loopholes, and IP-seeded honeypot redirection through CredShield. Over the next eighteen slides I'll walk you through the threat landscape, the system architecture, the implementation details, live screenshots, and the benchmark numbers. Why does this matter? Web security has evolved from passive 403 blocking to active intelligence gathering — DeceptiWAF bridges that gap. Let's get into it.

DeceptiWAF 02 / 19
Let me walk you through these stat cards. Sixty-five percent of web breaches still come from SQL injection and credential stuffing — the same vectors we've known about for fifteen years. Eighty percent of all attack traffic is fully automated; we're not fighting humans anymore, we're fighting scripts like sqlmap, nikto, and hydra. They don't get tired, they don't sleep, and they don't stop at the first 403. The four evasion tactics on the left are real payloads seen in the wild — multi-level URL encoding, HTML entity encoding, Unicode full-width characters, and inline SQL comment insertion. These are the exact payloads DeceptiWAF is benchmarked against. The bar chart on the right shows OWASP Top 10 breach distribution — injection alone accounts for thirty-two percent. Every minute spent blocking a bot is a minute taken from supporting real users — DeceptiWAF takes that operational tax and redirects it into threat intelligence. Basically, we made the bots do our homework for us.
PROBLEM · 03

The static 403 block is a feedback gift to attackers.

Traditional WAFs rely on regex rules and respond immediately with HTTP 403 — three structural flaws make this a liability.

DeceptiWAF 03 / 19
Three structural flaws — and each one is a direct consequence of the block-and-tell design pattern. First, immediate feedback: a 403 hands attackers instant confirmation that their payload was detected, so they iterate rule-by-rule until something slips through. Second, zero attacker friction — they lose nothing, switch IPs, and resume within milliseconds. Third, false-positive friction — when aggressive rules catch a legitimate user, that user suffers complete access loss and has no idea why. Look at the comparison strip: every row in the passive column becomes a liability, every row in the deception column becomes an asset. Attackers easily differentiate fake 404s by inspecting response headers, content-length, and server banners — but active deception returns realistic HTTP 200 responses with a full decoy application state, same login flow, same dashboard, same data shape. The old WAF playbook basically tells attackers exactly what not to do next — rude.
SOLUTION · 04

Don't block. Don't educate. Don't alert.
Just reroute.

Instead of returning 403 to suspicious users, DeceptiWAF silently routes malicious and brute-force traffic into an isolated, decoy student portal — the attacker never realizes they've been trapped, and the legitimate user never feels a thing.

DeceptiWAF 04 / 19
The core philosophy: block equals feedback, deceive equals intelligence. Each of the four pillars solves a distinct problem. AST lexical parsing catches what regex misses — it tokenizes SQL syntax structures, so comment insertion and whitespace tricks don't fool it. Multi-pass de-obfuscation handles layered encoding — URL decoding, HTML entities, Unicode NFKC normalization, and SQL comment stripping all run in sequence. The sliding-window rate limiter kills brute-force with strict per-IP windows — no boundary-burst escape. And CredShield turns brute-forcers into trapped attackers after three failed logins. Here's the key insight — WAFs provide real-time payload filtering but produce no threat intelligence; honeypots capture telemetry but typically sit outside the production request path. DeceptiWAF combines both: inline WAF filtering plus inline honeypot redirection, so every blocked attacker becomes a source of intelligence without any disruption to legitimate user flows. Basically, every WAF block used to be the end of the story — we made it the beginning.

DeceptiWAF 06 / 19
Let me walk the pipeline left-to-right. A request hits the rate limiter first — that's the cheapest rejection, an O(1) hash lookup. Then it goes to the WAF engine, which combines regex pattern matching with AST semantic inspection. Then CredShield checks: is this IP already trapped in the honeypot? If any stage rejects, the request exits early — that's the three branch outcomes you see below: 429, 403, or decoy 200. Only clean requests reach the application route handler, and clean requests skip the heavy honeypot logic entirely, which is why total overhead is under 1.5 milliseconds. One important detail — body parsers (urlencoded, JSON, cookieParser) run BEFORE the rate limiter and WAF so they can inspect req.body. That's critical because attack payloads often arrive in POST bodies, not just URLs. AST tokenization is sub-millisecond on typical payloads. We measured this — it's faster than your internet probably is.

DeceptiWAF 07 / 19
Three stages, three thresholds. Stage one uses three separate sliding windows tuned to different abuse patterns — login attempts, global throughput, and micro-bursts. The exact thresholds — fifteen per sixty seconds on login, sixty per sixty seconds globally, twenty per five seconds on micro-burst — come straight from lib/ratelimit.js. Stage two uses fifty-five pattern rules plus AST structural detections to accumulate a per-vector threat score; the block threshold is strictly score greater than four, so a single high-scoring hit — like a sqlmap user agent at score five — instantly blocks. Stage three is the deception switch. Three failed logins and the IP is silently moved into the honeypot. The threshold at three cleanly distinguishes human password typos from automated brute-force — a human might typo twice before slowing down, a bot fires fifty attempts in five seconds. Three is the smallest threshold that filters bots without ever trapping a legitimate user, and the thirty-minute auto-disarm TTL means even an edge case self-heals. Three strikes and you're in — the honeypot, that is.
ENGINE · 08

Tokenize first. Pattern-match second. Regex never.

descriptionlib/astWaf.js — regex is for emails. AST is for attackers.
Lexical Tokenizer — tokenizeSql()

Converts raw input into 7 typed tokens — COMMENT, STRING, NUMBER, OPERATOR, KEYWORD, IDENTIFIER, SYMBOL — so structure can be matched regardless of spacing or comments. SQL_KEYWORDS set covers 21 keywords (UNION, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER, EXEC, INFORMATION_SCHEMA, SLEEP, BENCHMARK, WAITFOR, XP_CMDSHELL, EXTRACTVALUE, UPDATEXML, AND, OR, FROM, WHERE, etc.).

the comment becomes a token of its own — UNION and SELECT still sit next to each other as keywords. cute trick, attackers.
DeceptiWAF 08 / 19
The AST tokenizer turns raw input into typed tokens — once you have tokens, pattern matching is trivial and immune to formatting tricks. Walk the example on the right: the comment `/**/` between UNION and SELECT is tokenized as a COMMENT, not as part of either keyword, so the pattern `KEYWORD KEYWORD` — UNION followed by SELECT — still matches cleanly. Compared to naive regex, regex breaks the moment attackers insert comments or whitespace variations like `UNION/*foo*/SELECT`. The AST tokenizer doesn't care about the syntax noise. Compared to deep learning or ML approaches, ML models introduce heavy latency — over fifty milliseconds per request — and produce false positives you can't debug. AST parsing runs in under half a millisecond with one hundred percent deterministic rules — every single block has an auditable reason. The DOM-side AST also catches XSS via dangerous tags, inline event handlers, and the javascript: protocol — that's three SQLi patterns plus three XSS pattern families, all scoring three or four. Regex is for emails. AST is for attackers.

grid_view Combinatorial Haystack Generator — buildHaystacks()

Generates the cartesian product of all decoded variants and tests rules against every one simultaneously. A single payload may pass through 4+ encoding layers — DeceptiWAF tests rules against the haystack, not the raw string.

raw → deepDecode → decodeHtmlEntities → normalizeUnicode → normalizeForSql → 4+ haystack variants tested

DeceptiWAF 09 / 19
Walk through each pass with the example. The key insight is that attackers layer these techniques — a payload might be URL-encoded twice, then HTML-entity-encoded, then Unicode-obfuscated, then SQL-comment-stuffed. Each pass alone is insufficient; the four-pass sequence peels every layer. The reason we test against all combinatorial variants is that attackers layer multiple obfuscation techniques simultaneously — testing rules against raw strings alone allows evasive payloads to slip through when only one layer is removed. buildHaystacks generates the cartesian product of all decoded variants and tests the rule engine against every single one — if any variant trips a rule, the request is blocked. This is brute-force defense against brute-force obfuscation. Also note that DeceptiWAF scans four input vectors per request — path, query params (skipping the token key so legitimate session tokens don't get flagged), body fields, and the User-Agent and Referer headers — so attackers can't sneak payloads through header channels. Attackers love layered encoding. We love layered decoding. It's a whole thing.

DeceptiWAF 10 / 19
Explain the three thresholds — login at fifteen requests per sixty seconds, global at sixty per sixty, and micro-burst at twenty per five — and how they cover three distinct abuse vectors. Walk through the visualization on the right: the sliding window moves continuously with `now`, so there's no boundary at which an attacker can double their rate. Compared to fixed windows — fixed windows allow double-rate burst spikes at window boundaries. For example, sixty requests at zero fifty-nine plus sixty at one zero zero equals one hundred twenty in one second, all quote unquote allowed by a naive counter. Compared to token buckets — token buckets allow initial burst dumps because the bucket starts full. Sliding window enforces strict micro-burst limits — max twenty requests per five seconds — at every moment, with no boundary artifacts. Also note that all three checks run in priority order on every request: burst first at five seconds, then login flood at sixty seconds on POST /login only, then global at sixty seconds. Fixed windows are like a security guard who clock-watches. Ours never blinks.

DeceptiWAF 11 / 19
Walk the state machine left to right. Attempts one and two look like normal failed logins — but DeceptiWAF is already watching, and the IP state silently moves from CLEAN to WATCHED. On attempt three, the IP state flips to HONEYPOT_ACTIVE and noteFailedLogin returns action activate. From attempt four onwards, every request from that IP is intercepted by CredShield: the auth check is skipped entirely, a deterministic fake profile is generated, a session is issued with the reserved sentinel username __honeypot__, and the attacker is served an HTTP 200 response that redirects to /dashboard — which serves honeypot.html, the decoy. Critically, the URL bar shows /dashboard?token=…, NOT /trap — there's an explicit /trap → /dashboard redirect in server.js to keep the URL bar clean. If an attacker tries legitimate credentials while trapped, CredShield intercepts all authentication requests from a trapped IP — the real auth handler is never called. Even a valid credential cannot reach production data once an IP is in HONEYPOT_ACTIVE state. Even correct passwords can't save you now. Beautiful.

psychology Why deterministic seeding (FNV-1a → mulberry32), not random?

Random profiles regenerate on every page refresh — a trapped attacker would notice the name changed and bail. The claimed-username hash keeps the decoy 100% consistent across sessions, so the attacker keeps digging. Note: honeypot.html and dashboard.html are byte-for-byte near-identical templates — only one console.error tag differs.

fnv1a(claimedUsername) → seed → mulberry32(seed) → all profile fields
DeceptiWAF 12 / 19
Walk the side-by-side: visually, the two dashboards are identical in structure — same header, same field layout, same course list shape, same Kalyani University branding. The only difference is the data: real on the left, fully synthetic on the right. The synthetic data is fully deterministic — every field is derived from an FNV-1a hash of the claimed username, fed into a mulberry32 PRNG. So the same claimed username always produces the same fake student. Why deterministic and not random? If a trapped attacker refreshes the page and sees a different student profile every time, they will immediately realize they're inside a honeypot and abandon the session. The hash-based profile keeps the decoy one hundred percent consistent across sessions and refreshes — the same attacker always sees Rohan Das, ECE, Semester four, and that consistency is what keeps them engaged. Critical point: the seed comes from the claimed username, NOT the IP address — so two attackers behind the same NAT router get two distinct decoy profiles, and a single attacker retrying with different usernames sees different fake students. Randomness is great for passwords. Terrible for lies.

The whole point of this slide is visual deception — both dashboards are byte-for-byte near-identical templates. Only one console dot error tag differs in the source code. Same Kalyani University branding, same nav bar, same KPI cards, same course ledger table shape, same 'Secured by DeceptiWAF' footer. The URL bar even shows the same path: slash dashboard. The avatar, name, branch, semester, CGPA, attendance, credits, dues, course list, grades — every field is fully synthetic on the right, but visually plausible. If you can spot the difference in under ten seconds, you're hired.

DeceptiWAF 14 / 19
This is the SOC Command Center at soc.html — the operational view of everything DeceptiWAF is doing in real time. The KPI strip up top rolls up events-per-minute, total WAF blocks, honeypot traps, rate-limited hits, and unique attacker IPs. The left column is the live telemetry feed — every WAF block, honeypot trap, and rate-limit event streams in as it happens. The middle column aggregates top attackers by IP with geo flags, and the right column shows currently-trapped IPs and the fake identity each has been assigned, plus a System Health panel confirming all five subsystems are online. Two important architectural notes: Socket.IO requires an admin-role session token in the handshake — students and honeypot-trapped users cannot subscribe to telemetry. And there are only TWO event channels — waf_event, which carries WAF blocks, flags, and rate-limit blocks tagged with kind:'ratelimit', and honeypot_event, for failed, activated, and trapped transitions. Compared to HTTP long-polling, WebSockets give us bidirectional, low-latency streaming with no HTTP overhead and no polling lag. No refresh button needed — the bad news streams itself.

PERSISTENCE · 16

Why SQLite WAL Mode?

  • Concurrent readers alongside zero-latency synchronous logging
  • No external network daemon dependencies (unlike Redis / MongoDB)
  • Single-file deployment — entire DB ships with the app at data/deceptiwaf.db
WAL · better-sqlite3 data/deceptiwaf.db
DeceptiWAF 16 / 19
Walk through each table. sessions holds authenticated session tokens and any decoy profile JSON assigned to a trapped IP — it backs the in-memory L1 cache plus SQLite L2 fallback pattern in server.js. events is the audit log — every WAF block, honeypot trap, and rate-limit event lands here with full context including payload hits, geo, server time, fingerprint, and user-agent. The seq column is a monotonic counter persisted across restarts so the SOC console can resume the feed without gaps. rate_limits is declared in the schema but never read or written — the rate limiter uses an in-memory Map for O(1) performance, and the table is reserved for future horizontal-scale persistence. SQLite WAL mode enables concurrent readers alongside zero-latency synchronous logging without requiring external network daemon dependencies like Redis or MongoDB. The WAF pipeline can write events on every request without blocking readers, and there's no separate database process to manage, restart, or secure. For a single-node inline WAF, this is the right trade-off: zero operational complexity, full ACID guarantees, and zero network hops on the hot path. Redis is great. Also: another thing to keep awake at 3am. We passed.

DeceptiWAF 17 / 19
Walk the KPI grid: latency overhead is the headline number — under 1.5ms per request means the WAF is effectively invisible to legitimate users. 55 pattern rules across four families — 17 SQLi, 17 XSS, 10 path traversal, 11 malicious user-agents — plus the AST structural detections on top. 47 test cases in test-waf.sh cover every category including 9 anti-evasion cases with multi-encoded payloads and 6 benign controls to verify the false-positive rate is zero. Honeypot isolation is 100% by construction — once an IP is in HONEYPOT_ACTIVE state, there is no code path in server.js that reaches the real auth handler; the credShield.isHoneypotActive(ip) check at the top of POST /login short-circuits to the trap path unconditionally. The anti-evasion row is highlighted because it's the most interesting: payloads like double-encoded UNION SELECT or full-width Unicode variants get rebuilt into a normalized haystack via buildHaystacks before pattern matching, so obfuscation doesn't help. Benchmarked using HTTP test suites firing concurrent requests against /, /login, /dashboard, and /test — each vector run multiple times to compute average detection scores and p99 latency. The only thing faster than our WAF is the attacker's regret.

This is the Cyber Range — the open-access attack simulator at /test, no auth required. Walk through the layout: the KPI strip up top tracks total launches, blocks, rate-limits, passes, and block efficiency percentage. The left column has three attack vector studios — SQLi, XSS, and path traversal — each with preset payload buttons; click one and the WAF reacts instantly. The right column has the de-obfuscation presets, malicious user-agent presets, and the headline feature: the CredShield brute-force demo. One button fires four sequential logins; the first three fail and arm the honeypot, and the fourth attempt lands the attacker in the trap with a fake identity. The bottom terminal shows every fired request with timestamp, HTTP status, and the rule that triggered it. This is the slide you'll likely demo live — fire a UNION SELECT in the SQLi studio, then jump back to the SOC console and watch the same event stream in. Basically a paintball range, but for SQL injection.
